intro: London's sound comes from the people who arrived and the rooms they built for themselves. Caribbean sound systems in Brixton and Notting Hill seeded lovers rock in the 1970s, then pirate radio and basement raves carried jungle, UK garage, grime and dubstep out of the estates.

The underground now meets in member-funded and volunteer-run spaces. Cafe OTO in Dalston books free improvisation, noise and outsider folk, IKLECTIK moved its experimental programme to Peckham Levels in 2025, and Resonance FM broadcasts art radio on 104.4. South London's shops and small labels keep lovers rock, dub and new jazz in circulation.

intro: Lagos turned jùjú and fuji into the music of its streets and parties. Fuji grew out of wéré, the songs that wake the faithful before dawn in Ramadan, and Fela Kuti built Afrobeat at his Shrine with drummer Tony Allen. In the 1980s small studios cut boogie and disco records that diggers still hunt for.

Away from the arenas, the alté generation has made slower, stranger records since the late 2010s, and parties such as Element House and Group Therapy are growing an electronic underground. Bogobiri House in Ikoyi and the Jazzhole shop keep the listening-room culture going.
buy: Awolowo Road, Ikoyi: records, books and gigs for over 30 years

intro: Congolese rumba was born here and in Brazzaville across the river, when Cuban son records arriving in the 1940s were remade with Congolese guitars and Lingala lyrics. It sped up into soukous and ndombolo in the bars of Matonge and Bandal.

Kinshasa's underground builds its own instruments. Konono Nº1 amplified the likembe thumb piano with car parts, KOKOKO! play home-made gear, and the KinAct collective, founded by Eddy Ekete in 2015, turns street performance into music: their LP Kinshasa in Action came out on Nyege Nyege Tapes. Their base, Ndaku ya La vie est belle in Matonge, is a self-run arts space and home of the KinAct festival.
adopted: Bazombo musicians from the Angolan border

intro: Bamako is where the griot traditions of the old Mande empire met electric guitars, horns and Cuban records. In the 1970s the Rail Band played the station's Buffet Hôtel de la Gare, launching Salif Keita and Mory Kanté.

The new underground comes out of home studios. In Sotuba, producer Gaspa records the city's young rappers and singers, and his Gaspa Show #1, released on the Blanc Manioc label in 2021, put Papson, Wari First, RG Gang, Kal B, Meslaa and Lil Boula on one record.
buy: Market stalls by the Grand Mosque

intro: In the late 1960s and early 70s Addis Ababa's nightclubs and its army, police and imperial guard bands created 'Swinging Addis', Ethiopian scales played with horns, organ and soul rhythm sections. Mulatu Astatke mixed them with jazz into ethio-jazz, and small labels like Amha Records recorded it before the 1974 revolution shut the clubs.

The scene today is small, live and moving fast. Moseb Music Center hosts Tasew Wendim's Monday sessions, Fendika keeps the azmari tradition going at events in Bole, and the Kebelezero crew makes electronic music from Ethiopian sounds and runs Kebele Radio with Sheger Studios. The Lab runs a DJ series and Fabrica opened in late 2025.
listen: azmari music, now at events in Bole
buy: by the old bus station, making and selling tapes and CDs since the 1970s

intro: Johannesburg's townships made marabi in the 1920s shebeens, kwela pennywhistles in the 1950s streets and the township jazz of Sophiatown, before the area was bulldozed from 1955. Mbaqanga, kwaito and, in the 2010s, amapiano all grew from township parties.

The independent jazz scene meets in small rooms. Untitled Basement in Braamfontein, run by the Artivist group, hosts DJ Kenzhero and The Globalist and the Beats By Her series, with pianist Nduduzo Makhathini, singer Zoë Modiga, Bokani Dyer and Linda Sikhakhane in its circle. VOW FM, the Wits campus station, was named campus station of the year in 2024.
buy: South African disco, bubblegum and jazz

intro: Fado has been sung in the taverns of Alfama and Mouraria since the 19th century, and Cape Verdean morna and funaná and Angolan semba arrived with migrants, above all after the 1974 revolution.

The underground lives on the city's edges. DJ Marfox and the Príncipe label took batida, the kuduro-born sound of the outer neighbourhoods, into clubs worldwide, and DIY rooms such as Outra Cena in Marvila, Desterro, Vago and Damas keep the dancing going after Musicbox closed in 2025. Rádio Quântica, online since 2015, and Violet's naive label grew from the same scene.
listen: Cape Verdean and Lusophone dance nights

intro: Salvador was Brazil's main slave-trade port, and its music keeps the country's deepest African roots: Candomblé drums, capoeira and samba de roda. In 1974 Ilê Aiyê became the first bloco afro, and in the 1980s Olodum created samba-reggae.

The current underground is party culture. Independent nights like MATRIZ and Baile Charme at Casa da Felicidade, MANIFESTO at the Cine Teatro Solar Boa Vista in Brotas, Embrazza's pagodão sets and Brega a Dois at A Marujada mix pagodão baiano and brega with club music. BaianaSystem took the guitarra baiana and sound-system bass from the same streets.
Havana's dance halls turned country forms into danzón, son, mambo and cha-cha-chá, and rumba grew in the Afro-Cuban yards of Havana and Matanzas.

An experimental underground has grown on laptops and borrowed gear. Æterna Fragma, Buffalo Attack, Blastterz and daku make noise, ambient and club music, released abroad on labels like Ultramar, set up in 2025, and the Eyeife and Human Noises festivals bring them together. La Madriguera gives them a stage, and Fábrica de Arte Cubano did until it closed temporarily in June 2026 for lack of energy.
buy: label releasing the Cuban experimental scene

intro: Colombia's rhythms, cumbia, vallenato, champeta and currulao, come from the coasts. Bogotá is where they meet and get remixed.

Its underground has two families. One digs into the coast: Frente Cumbiero, Meridian Brothers and the Cumbia Bestial party, launched at La Mecánica in 2025 with Divino Colapso and Conjunto Media Luna. The other is club music, from drum and bass at RE.SET to collectives like Autonotek, Liquid Mood, Womandbass and Bogotrax.
adopted: Bomba Estéreo's singer, born in Santa Marta

intro: In 1950s Kingston, sound systems fought with American R&B records, then started recording local musicians to beat each other: ska, rocksteady and reggae followed. King Tubby in Waterhouse and Lee 'Scratch' Perry at his Black Ark turned the mixing desk into an instrument and invented dub.

Sound system culture still runs on the street. Rae Town's Sunday dance plays oldies and lovers rock in the old fishing village, Dub Club on Skyline Drive spins roots and dub above the city, and Inner City Dub runs downtown. Orange Street, once called Beat Street, still has record shops.
listen: Nation Lounge, Spanish Town Road, Mondays
buy: Orange Street, Augustus Pablo's shop, revived by his son Addis Pablo

intro: In the 1960s and 70s Erkin Koray, Cem Karaca and Selda Bağcan plugged Anatolian folk melodies into psychedelic rock, while migrants from the countryside filled the city with arabesk.

Today's independent scene runs through Kadıköy and Beyoğlu. Bands such as Jakuzi, Kilink, Palmiyeler and Adamlar, producers Nilipek and Pitohui and collectives IDGK and Boykot play rooms like Blind, Karga, Arkaoda and Yuva. Apaçık Radyo carries the independent voice online after Açık Radyo lost its FM licence in 2024.

Georgian polyphonic singing was among the first traditions UNESCO recognised, in 2001. Since the mid-2010s Tbilisi has also been a techno city whose clubs double as a protest movement, from the 2018 rallies after police raided them to the club strikes of late 2024.

The pressure shows. TES closed in January 2026 and Tbili Orgia ended with a final party, both carrying on through the Meteor studio, while Bassiani and Left Bank stay open and Mutant Radio broadcasts from a former power station. DJs Esi, Wesley Wise and Devi came up through these rooms.
From the 1950s Beirut was the stage and studio of the Arab world, and Ziad Rahbani later mixed Arabic music with jazz and funk.

Its independent scene grew after the civil war around experimental and alternative music: the Irtijal festival of improvised music, Raed Yassin's Annihaya, Rabih Beaini's Morphine label, Fadi Tabbal's Tunefork Studios and the Ruptured label, home to Munma, Mayssa Jallad, Charbel Haber, Youmna Saba, Yara Asmar and Julia Sabra. Many venues have reopened since the 2020 port explosion.
buy: rock, soul and a strong Arabic collection

intro: Bombay's film songs were arranged and played by Goan jazz musicians like Chic Chocolate, Anthony Gonsalves and Frank Fernand, and composers such as R.D. Burman borrowed from jazz, funk and rock.

The independent scene lives in small rooms. antiSOCIAL, The Quarter, G5A and Bonobo in Bandra host bands, DJs and jazz, The Habitat in Khar runs open mics, and Boxout.fm broadcasts as India's online community radio. Gully rap, sparked by Naezy and Divine, came out of the neighbourhoods.
Jakarta mixes the music of an archipelago: keroncong from the Mardijker community of Kampung Tugu, the Betawi gambang kromong and, from the 1970s, Rhoma Irama's rock-guitar dangdut.

It also has one of Asia's loudest DIY scenes. Rossi Musik in Cilandak hosts punk, hardcore and noise shows, and Vacation Records, five friends running parties, a record shop and a label, turn lounges and restaurants into clubs for music the big rooms won't book.
Naples gave the world canzone napoletana, and in the 1970s Pino Daniele, James Senese's Napoli Centrale and Tullio De Piscopo mixed it with blues, funk and jazz.

The independent city runs through its social centres. Officina 99 and DAMM in Montesanto grew the scene of Almamegretta's dub, 'A 67, Clan Vesuvio and KTM, and Daniele Sepe has spent decades mixing tammurriata, jazz and protest songs. The masked singer Liberato and the Napoli Segreta compilations have pointed new ears at the city.

Jazz was born here out of brass bands, ragtime, blues and Creole music, and the Sunday gatherings of enslaved Africans in Congo Square are remembered as its deepest root. Allen Toussaint and The Meters later wrote the rules of funk.

The street keeps it independent. Brass bands like the Treme Brass Band, Hot 8, Stooges and Young Groovy play neighbourhood bars such as the Candlelight Lounge and Bullet's Sports Bar, second lines roll on Sundays, and bounce and Mardi Gras Indian chants carry the city's own rhythms. WWOZ and the freeform WTUL broadcast them.

Medellín was the factory of Colombia's tropical music. Discos Fuentes moved here from Cartagena in 1954, and with Codiscos and Sonolux the city's studios cut coastal cumbia and porro next to the salsa of Fruko y sus Tesos and the Afro-tropical records of Wganda Kenya and Afrosound. Tango came too: Carlos Gardel died in a plane crash here in 1935, and Salón Málaga downtown has played tango since 1957.

The underground came out of the barrios. Punk and metal crews grew up in 1980s Castilla during the city's worst years, a story told in Caliche's book Mala Hierba, and today Comuna 13's Casa Kolacho collective runs the free Manifiesto hip hop festival. El Club del Jazz in El Palo holds Thursday jams in a 50-person room, and Teatro Matacandelas, home of the first MedeJazz in 1997, books experimental and heavy bills.
